title: Scramble String
statement:
A string is *scrambled* by this recursive process:

- A string of length 1 is left as it is.
- A longer string is cut at any position into two non-empty parts `x` and `y` (so the string is `x + y`). The two parts are then either kept in order (`x + y`) or exchanged (`y + x`), and each part is itself scrambled by the same process, independently of the other.

Every cut position and every keep-or-exchange choice is free, so one string can produce many scrambles (including itself). Given two strings `s1` and `s2` of equal length, return `true` if some sequence of choices turns `s1` into `s2`, and `false` otherwise.
constraints: s1 and s2 contain only lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

Look at the top-level cut of a scramble. If `s1` was cut after `k` characters, its first `k` characters ended up either at the front of `s2` (kept) or at the back of `s2` (exchanged), and each piece must itself be a scramble of the matching piece of `s2`. So "is this piece of `s1` a scramble of that piece of `s2`?" is the real question, and a piece is fully described by its start in `s1`, its start in `s2` and its length. Trying every cut recursively repeats the same pieces exponentially often; a table over `(len, i, j)` answers each one once.

## Approach

1. Let `dp[len][i][j]` mean: `s1` from `i` with length `len` can be scrambled into `s2` from `j` with length `len`.
2. Length 1: `dp[1][i][j]` is true exactly when `s1[i] === s2[j]`.
3. For each `len` from 2 to `n`, each valid `i` and `j`, try every cut `k` from 1 to `len - 1`:
   - `keep`: the first `k` characters match the first `k` of the `s2` piece, and the remaining `len - k` match the rest.
   - `swap`: the first `k` characters match the **last** `k` of the `s2` piece, and the remaining `len - k` match its start.
4. If either holds for some `k`, set the entry to true and stop trying cuts.
5. Return `dp[n][0][0]`.

## Example 1, step by step

`s1 = "great"`, `s2 = "rgeat"`. At length 2, `"gr"` versus `"rg"` (`i = 0`, `j = 0`) fails `keep` (`g` vs `r`) but passes `swap` (`g` vs `g`, `r` vs `r`). At length 3, `"eat"` versus `"eat"` (`i = 2`, `j = 2`) passes `keep`. At length 5 with `k = 2`, `keep` needs `dp[2][0][0]` (`"gr"` to `"rg"`) and `dp[3][2][2]` (`"eat"` to `"eat"`); both are true, so the answer is `true`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n⁴): O(n³) table entries, each trying up to `n` cuts.
- Space: O(n³) for the table.

## Pitfalls

- In the `swap` case the `s2` offsets are easy to get wrong: the first part of `s1` lines up with `s2` starting at `j + len - k`, and the second part with `s2` starting at `j`.
- Fill the table by increasing `len`; every check reads only shorter lengths, which must already be final.
- Having the same letters is necessary but not enough: `"abcd"` and `"bdac"` use the same letters yet are not scrambles.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | length of both strings |
| `dp[len][i][j]` | whether `s1`'s piece at `i` of length `len` scrambles into `s2`'s piece at `j` |
| `len` | length of the pieces being compared |
| `i`, `j` | start of the piece in `s1` and in `s2` |
| `k` | length of the first part of the `s1` piece at the cut |
| `keep`, `swap` | whether the cut works with the parts kept in order or exchanged |

narration.2: Both strings have the same length n.
narration.3: dp[len][i][j] will say whether s1's piece at i of length len scrambles into s2's piece at j.
narration.6: A single character can only stay itself, so the characters must be equal.
narration.9: Build longer pieces from shorter ones, shortest first.
narration.10: Every start in s1 where a piece of this length fits...
narration.11: ...against every start in s2 where it fits.
narration.12: Try each cut that leaves both parts non-empty; k is the length of the first part.
narration.13: Kept in order: the first k characters match the start of the s2 piece and the rest match the rest.
narration.14: Exchanged: the first k characters match the end of the s2 piece and the rest match its start.
narration.16: Mark this pair of pieces as scrambles of each other.
narration.17: No need to try more cuts.
narration.23: The whole of s1 against the whole of s2.
